appraisal_events.evidence: chaque château... a sa dame, ou sa fée; the narrator imagines her as the 'suzeraine du lieu et dame du lac' whose face and words should hold the antique, legendary charm of an ancient forest domain reaching back before Notre-Dame de Paris was built.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's remembered imagination mythologizes Mme de Guermantes into a legendary feudal fairy-suzeraine of immense antiquity and grandeur, elevating her far beyond an ordinary aristocrat.

appraisal_events.evidence: Saint-Loup lui avait appris que le château ne s'appelait Guermantes que depuis le XVIIe siècle; les tapisseries étaient de Boucher, achetées au XIXe siècle, placées dans 'un fort vilain salon drapé d'andrinople et de peluche.'
appraisal_events.explanation: Saint-Loup's matter-of-fact historical corrections strip away the medieval, fairy-tale grandeur the narrator had imagined around Mme de Guermantes, replacing it with a comparatively recent and even tacky reality.

status_effects.explanation: In the narrator's imagination she is elevated to legendary, near-mythic feudal-aristocratic grandeur.
Saint-Loup's factual revelations deflate that imagined grandeur down to a more recent, unglamorous aristocratic reality.
Saint-Loup is positioned as the authoritative source of corrective factual knowledge that overrides the narrator's romantic fantasy.

ambiguities: The 'elevation' of Mme de Guermantes in E1 is entirely internal to the narrator's remembered imagination rather than an external social judgment endorsed as objectively true; this affects how the positive status movement should be read (perceived/mythic prestige rather than actual social standing).
